ledger.claim_text: Three miles beneath the Pacific Ocean, sunken Soviet nuclear submarine K-129 rested at 16,500 feet depth carrying nuclear missiles and cryptographic gear.
ledger.source_title: CIA Declassified Studies in Intelligence: Project Azorian - The Story of the Hughes Glomar Explorer
ledger.publisher: Central Intelligence Agency (Center for the Study of Intelligence)
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: K-129 sank in March 1968 at 40°06'N, 179°57'E at a depth of 16,500 feet (over 3 miles) with three R-21 ballistic nuclear missiles, two nuclear torpedoes, and cipher materials.

ledger.claim_text: The CIA enlisted eccentric billionaire Howard Hughes to build the 618-foot Hughes Glomar Explorer under the cover story of deep-sea manganese nodule mining.
ledger.source_title: National Security Archive: The Project Azorian Declassified Dossier
ledger.publisher: The National Security Archive / George Washington University
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Sun Shipbuilding built the 618-foot vessel for Summa Corporation, Hughes's holding company, maintaining a public facade of commercially mining manganese nodules from the seabed.

ledger.claim_text: Inside the ship was a hidden moon pool housing Clementine: a multi-million-pound mechanical steel claw designed to envelop the submarine hull.
ledger.source_title: US Naval Institute: The Hughes Glomar Explorer and the Recovery of K-129
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Lockheed Missiles and Space designed the 180-foot Capture Vehicle (nicknamed Clementine) with articulated hydraulic capture arms to envelop the 2,700-ton submarine hull.

ledger.claim_text: Lowering the claw required connecting 3 miles of heavy steel drill pipe supporting over 16 million pounds of dead weight in violent ocean currents.
ledger.source_title: Project Azorian: The Central Intelligence Agency and the Cold War
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Approx 600 sections of 30-foot oilfield pipe were connected on a gimbaled heave-compensated derrick, supporting dynamic tensile loads exceeding 16 million pounds.

ledger.claim_text: At 9,000 feet depth, claw fingers suffered catastrophic structural failure, snapping and dropping two-thirds of the submarine back to the seabed.
ledger.source_title: CIA Declassified Monograph: Mission Azorian Mechanical Evaluation
ledger.publisher: CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: On August 1, 1974, multiple mechanical tines suffered brittle fracture under load at ~9,000 feet depth; the aft two-thirds of K-129 broke away and fell back into the abyss.

ledger.claim_text: The recovered bow section contained two nuclear-tipped torpedoes and 6 Soviet crew members who received a formal military burial at sea with naval honors.
ledger.source_title: US Department of Defense / CIA White House Memorandum: Soviet Burial Film Handover
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Two nuclear torpedoes were safely recovered; six Soviet submariners were interred at sea with a formal ceremony, bilingual prayers, the Soviet national anthem, and full honors.

ledger.claim_text: The mission birthed the famous 'neither confirm nor deny' legal doctrine known as the Glomar Response still used today.
ledger.source_title: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit: Phillippi v. CIA (546 F.2d 1009)
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: In response to FOIA requests regarding the Glomar Explorer, the CIA refused to confirm or deny records, establishing the landmark 'Glomar response' in federal administrative law.

ledger.claim_text: Total mission costs reached approximately $800 million in 1974 dollars, equivalent to approximately $4.0 billion in modern inflation-adjusted value.
ledger.source_title: US General Accounting Office: Financial Audit & Historical Valuations of Project Azorian
ledger.supporting_excerpt_or_notes: Total program expenditures were approximately $800 million across 1970–1975, which inflates to over $4.0 billion in 2026 currency value.
